summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office has produced the most detailed public accounting of artificial intelligence use inside the federal government. Per GAO, twenty of twenty-three major federal agencies reported roughly 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three agencies reported no uses for AI at all. Of those 1,200 cases, only about 200 involved AI that was actually in production and currently being used, meaning the large majority remained in planning phases. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of use cases. Reported applications included analyzing drone photographs, examining camera and radar feeds to identify border activities, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, alongside more routine uses such as identifying information security threats and facilitating the review of large datasets.

GAO found serious gaps in how agencies are tracking and managing these deployments. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, but the remaining fifteen had instances of incomplete or inaccurate data, including inventories missing required elements such as AI life cycle stage. Two agencies submitted inventories that included uses later determined not to be AI at all. Ten of the twenty-three agencies fully implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. The Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, a gap GAO identified as preventing consistent management of AI risk across the federal government.

On the funding side, the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI, per GAO. The General Services Administration established an AI Center of Excellence, and the Department of Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards, making those two agencies the furthest along among the examples GAO reviewed. The Office of Personnel Management had not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work, a practical obstacle to building the workforce the government will need to operate these systems.

The regulatory and legislative environment surrounding government AI use is unusually active. Per the law tracking on this site, 2,429 AI bills have been introduced across 53 jurisdictions and are updated daily from LegiScan, reflecting the pace at which state legislatures are moving to define rules for AI in public-sector and other contexts. OECD.AI monitors more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives across member and partner countries, tracking national strategies, public-sector initiatives, and ethical frameworks, and the OECD AI Principles emphasize that trustworthy AI systems should be fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure, and safe. Oxford Insights produces the Government AI Readiness Index, which scores countries on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption and serves as the standard cross-national comparison tool in this space.

Stanford HAI's annual AI Index tracks government AI through the lens of legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, and notes that while AI capabilities and investment are accelerating, the governance frameworks needed to manage the technology are falling behind. For an organization deciding whether to deploy AI in or alongside government operations, the GAO record suggests the federal government is still in early stages, with real deployments outnumbered by plans, compliance requirements not yet uniformly met, and acquisition guidance still missing. The sheer volume of state legislation means that the regulatory landscape any practitioner must navigate is broad, fast-moving, and varies considerably by jurisdiction.
